rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited, unattributed poetic line attests the root saḥaqa; the author says the verb is triliteral, so no omitted element is needed to derive suḥq.
rows.anchor: وتسحقه ريح الصبا كل مسحق

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the phrase as God crushing them thoroughly, meaning that He removed them far away.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أي أسحقهم الله سحقا، أي باعدهم بعدا

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi says the expected verbal noun is isḥāq, with deletion in the form used; the author rejects needing this deletion.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي: القياس إسحاقا، فجاء المصدر على الحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have sukūn on ḥāʾ in suḥqan; ʿAli, Abu Jaʿfar, and al-Kisaʾi (with a variant transmission) read it with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بسكون الحاء وعلي وأبو جعفر والكسائي، بخلاف عن أبي الحرث عنه: بضمها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya takes suḥqan as an accusative curse against them; although the judgment is already fixed, its execution is future, so it is phrased as a prayer with an implied verb.
rows.anchor: فسحقا: نصبا على جهة الدعاء عليهم، وجاز ذلك فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says an accomplished event would normally take nominative, citing the threats and greetings in the Qurʾan as examples.
rows.anchor: وإن وقع وثبت، فالوجه فيه الرفع، كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fearing God unseen means either fearing the reported resurrection and its events, or fearing Him beyond people's sight in private.
rows.anchor: يخشون ربهم بالغيب: أي الذي أخبروا به من أمر المعاد وأحواله، أو غائبين عن أعين الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates private remembrance with the report of a person who remembers God alone and weeps.
rows.anchor: ورجل ذكر الله خاليا ففاضت عيناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address in “conceal your speech” is directed to all people; Ibn ʿAbbas gives as its occasion some polytheists telling one another to whisper so Muhammad's God would not hear.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وسببه أن بعض المشركين قال لبعض: أسروا قولكم لا يسمعكم إله محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes min as the object of “Who created?” and reads the interrogative as denying that the Creator lacks knowledge of His creation and its hidden and visible matters.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن من مفعول، والمعنى: أينتفي علمه بمن خلق

rows.speaker: بعض النحاة
rows.claim: Some grammarians instead make min the subject and omit the object: would the Creator not know your secret and public speech? The question rebukes that suggestion.
rows.anchor: وأجاز بعض النحاة أن يكون من فاعلا والمفعول محذوف، كأنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this intransitive root becomes transitive either with the causative hamza or with doubling, illustrated by two Qurʾanic forms.
rows.anchor: وإنما تعدى بالهمزة كقوله: وتذل من تشاء ، وإما بالتضعيف لقوله: وذللناها لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya analyzes dhalūl as faʿūl with passive-participle meaning, like rakūb and ḥalūb.
rows.anchor: والذلول فعول بمعنى مفعول، أي مذلولة، فهي كركوب وحلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Ibn ʿAtiyya's passive-participle analysis because the base verb is intransitive; transitivity requires the causative hamza or doubling.
rows.anchor: وليس بمعنى مفعول لأن فعله قاصر، وإنما تعدى بالهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to walk on the earth means to travel through it and earn one's livelihood.
rows.anchor: فامشوا في مناكبها: أمر بالتصرف فيها والاكتساب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، وقتادة، وبشر بن كعب
rows.claim: They explain the earth's manākib as its extremities, namely its mountains.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وقتادة وبشر بن كعب: أطرافها، وهي الجبال

rows.speaker: الفراء، والكلبي، ومنذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: They explain manākib as the earth's sides, comparing it to a person's two sides.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء والكلبي ومنذر بن سعيد: جوانبها، ومنكبا الرجل: جانباه

rows.speaker: الحسن والسدي
rows.claim: They explain the term as the earth's edge and its passes.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن والسدي: طرفها وفجاجها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads walking on the shoulders as an image of extreme subjugation: the camel's shoulders are too delicate for a rider to tread, yet the earth is subdued enough for this.
rows.anchor: والمشي في مناكبها مثل لفرط التذليل ومجازوته الغاية

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God made travel through the earth's mountains easy, which shows especially complete subjugation.
rows.anchor: سهل لكم السلوك في جبالها فهو أبلغ التذليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection is to God, who will question people about their gratitude for this blessing.
rows.anchor: وإليه النشور: أي البعث، فيسألكم عن شكر هذه النعمة عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary in the two hamzas of a-amintum: Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and al-Bazzi ease the second; Abu ʿAmr and Qalun insert an alif; Qunbul changes the first to wāw; other transmissions and readers have further variants.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وأبو عمرو والبزي: أأمنتم بتحقيق الأولى وتسهيل الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Who is in heaven” is figurative, since rational proof establishes that God is not confined to a direction; the implied referent is His kingdom, which is everywhere, with heaven singled out for its angels, throne, preserved tablet, and descending decrees.
rows.anchor: هذا مجاز، وقد قام البرهان العقلي على أن تعالى ليس بمتحيز في جهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation casts the wording in terms of the polytheists' anthropomorphic belief: it means the one whom they claim is in heaven, though God transcends place.
rows.anchor: أو جاء هذا على طريق اعتقادهم، إذ كانوا مشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations make min stand for the Creator of those in heaven, the angels, or Gabriel, the angel charged with causing the earth to sink and similar acts.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من على حذف مضاف، أي خالق من في السماء. وقيل: من هم الملائكة. وقيل: جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading takes min in the sense of “above,” meaning supremacy in power rather than a location.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من بمعنى على، ويراد بالعلو القهر والقدرة لا بالمكان

rows.speaker: أهل التحرير
rows.claim: Al-Taḥrīr states a consensus that “in heaven” cannot mean literal residence there; even anthropomorphists who place God on the Throne do not say He is in heaven.
rows.anchor: وفي التحرير: الإجماع منعقد على أنه ليس في السماء بمعنى الاستقرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened sinking is the earth's descent below; tamūr means it goes or waves like dust driven by wind.
rows.anchor: وهو ذهابها سفلا، فإذا هي تمور: أي تذهب أو تتموج، كما يذهب التراب في الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to al-Isrāʾ for the meaning of ḥāṣib; nadhīr and nakīr are verbal nouns meaning warning and denial.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم شرح الحاصب في سورة الإسراء، والنذير والنكير مصدران بمعنى الإنذار والإنكار

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Ḥassān ibn Thābit's verse uses nadhīr in the sense of a warning.
rows.anchor: وقال حسان بن ثابت: فأنذر مثلها نصحا قريشا ... من الرحمن إن قبلت نذير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warsh retains the yāʾ in nadhīrī and nakīrī, while the other six canonical readers omit it.
rows.anchor: وأثبت ورش ياء نذيري ونكيري، وحذفها باقي السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning of a possible sinking and hailstorm, the passage turns to the birds as a sign and as evidence that idols cannot do this; the hailstorm also recalls the birds that destroyed the People of the Elephant and warns Quraysh of the same possibility.
rows.anchor: نبههم على الاعتبار بالطير وما أحكم من خلقها، وعن عجز آلهتهم عن شيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāffāt are birds spreading their wings as though still; yaqbidhna means they draw their wings against their sides, alternating between the two states to rest.
rows.anchor: صافات: باسطة أجنحتها صافتها حتى كأنها ساكنة، ويقبضن: ويضممن الأجنحة إلى جوانبهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun ṣāffāt is followed by the verb yaqbidhna because the verb has the noun's meaning; the reverse order is also eloquent, though al-Suhayli calls it poor.
rows.anchor: وعطف الفعل على الاسم لما كان في معناه، ومثله قوله تعالى: فالمغيرات صبحا فأثرن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari describes extended wings as the basic state of flight, like swimming with limbs stretched; wing strokes are temporary and aid movement.
rows.anchor: وأما القبض فطارىء على البسط للاستظهار به على التحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says birds are held by God's power and rejects reducing this to wing shape, body design, or weight.
rows.anchor: إن أثقل الأشياء إذا أراد إمساكها في الهواء واستعلاءها إلى العرش كان ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority lighten the mīm of yumassikuhunna, while al-Zuhri doubles it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ما يمسكهن مخففا. والزهري مشددا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority assimilate the mīm of am into man; am here means “rather,” and the interrogative asks who could support the people if God punished them.
rows.anchor: وأم هنا بمعنى بل خاصة لأن الذي بعدها هو اسم استفهام في موضع رفع على الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Likewise, no one could provide for them if God withheld His provision.
rows.anchor: وكذلك من هو رازقكم إن أمسك رزقه، والمعنى: لا أحد ينصركم ولا يرزقكم

rows.speaker: طلحة
rows.claim: Talha reads am with a light mīm moved onto the following one; al-Lawāmiʿ paraphrases the question as a rebuke about whether the army or provider can help.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: أهذا الذي هو جند لكم ينصركم، أم الذي يرزقكم؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They persisted in arrogance and rebellion, fleeing from truth because it was burdensome.
rows.anchor: بل لجوا: تمادوا، في عتو: في تكبر وعناد، ونفور: شراد عن الحق لثقله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may refer to their idols.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا إشارة إلى أصنامهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the verse describes the Resurrection: unbelievers walk on their faces while believers walk upright; on this view the image is literal.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة نزلت مخبرة عن حال القيامة، وأن الكفار يمشون فيها على وجوههم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In a report answering how an unbeliever can walk on his face, the Prophet says the One who made him walk on his feet in this world can make him walk on his face in the next; the author says Qatada's reading is literal.
rows.anchor: إن الذي أمشاه في الدنيا على رجليه قادر أن يمشيه في الآخرة على وجهه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ومجاهد، والضحاك
rows.claim: They take the walking as a general metaphor for the disbeliever and believer in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو مجاز، ضرب مثلا للكافر والمؤمن في الدنيا. فقيل: عام، وهو قول ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A separate report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the comparison concerns Abu Jahl and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: نزلت في أبي جهل والرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view places the verse about Abu Jahl and Hamza; the unbeliever's confused doctrine is like a blind person stumbling, while the believer follows a clear, easy path with a settled heart.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في أبي جهل وحمزة، والمعنى أن الكافر في اضطرابه وتعسفه في عقيدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukibban is a circumstantial accusative from akabba, which is intransitive; kabb is transitive, and its hamza marks entering a state or becoming so.
rows.anchor: ومكبا: حال من أكب، وهو لا يتعدى، وكب متعد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari claims no form on the afʿala pattern is a direct responsive form; the author criticizes this claim as ignorance of Sibawayh's text.
rows.anchor: ولا شيء من بناء افعل مطوعا، ولا يتقن نحو هذا إلا حملة كتاب سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author attacks al-Zamakhshari for repeatedly boasting of Sibawayh while missing passages, and notes that Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf ibn Maʿzuz wrote a book listing his errors and ignorance.
rows.anchor: وكم من نص في كتاب سيبويه عمي بصره وبصيرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahdā appears to be a comparative of guidance; the question is rhetorical, since every listener would answer that the upright walker on a straight path is better guided.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاستفهام لا تراد حقيقته، بل المراد منه أن كل سامع يجيب بأن الماشي سويا على صراط مستقيم أهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qalīlan is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; mā is extra, and tashkurūn may begin a new clause or be an anticipated circumstantial clause, meaning they give little thanks.
rows.anchor: وانتصب قليلا على أنه نعت لمصدر محذوف، وما زائدة، وتشكرون مستأنف أو حال مقدرة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the unbelievers give some thanks, but it is little and useless; alternatively, “little” may idiomatically mean no thanks at all.
rows.anchor: ظاهر أنهم يشكرون قليلا، وما عسى أن يكون للكافرين شكر، وهو قليل غير نافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dharākum means He spread you; al-ḥashr is resurrection, and the promise in question is the promised Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ذرأكم: بثكم، والحشر: البعث، والوعد المشار إليه هو وعد يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When they see the promised punishment near, zalfa means proximity or something near; al-Hasan says they see it plainly, and Ibn Zayd says it is present.
rows.anchor: فلما رأوه زلفة: أي رأوا العذاب وهو الموعود به، زلفة: أي قربا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical analysis supplies “a place” before zalfa, making it an adverbial expression.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير مكانا ذا زلفة، فانتصب على الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their faces looked dreadful and gloomy, darkened as if they were being led to execution.
rows.anchor: وظهر فيها السوء والكآبة، وغشيها السواد كمن يساق إلى القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use a plain kasra in sīʾat; a group of named readers use an imāla-like ḍamma coloring.
rows.anchor: وأخلص الجمهور كسرة السين، وأشمها الضم أبو جعفر والحسن وأبو رجاء وشيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ones who say “this is what you used to call for” are the keepers of Hell and others who rebuke them.
rows.anchor: وقيل لهم، أي تقول لهم الزبانية ومن يوبخهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: With the majority's doubled, open-dāl reading tadʿūn, al-Hasan explains it as their claim that neither Paradise nor Hell exists.
rows.anchor: فقيل: من الدعوى. قال الحسن: تدعون أنه لا جنة ولا نار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation derives tadʿūn from calling: they were asking for or hastening the punishment; a sukūn-dāl reading supports this sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تطلبون وتستعجلون، وهو من الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several readers, including Abu Rajaʾ, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatada, and Yaʿqub, read tadʿūn with a still dāl; further named transmissions also use this reading.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة ابن أبي عبلة وأبي زيد وعصمة عن أبي بكر والأصمعي عن نافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers used to invoke ruin on the Prophet and his Companions or conspire to kill them; the Prophet is told that whether God destroys him or grants him victory, they cannot escape the punishment caused by their unbelief.
rows.anchor: روي أن الكفار كانوا يدعون على الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وأصحابه بالهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning mercy, the passage names the means of salvation: faith and entrusting oneself to God.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر ما به النجاة وهو الإيمان والتفويض إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read fastaʿlamūn with second-person tāʾ; al-Kisaʾi reads it with third-person yāʾ, matching the preceding reference to the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فستعلمون بتاء الخطاب، والكسائي: بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After general punishment, the text names loss of water, which sustains life, as a specific punishment; the author refers to al-Kahf for ghawr and al-Muʾminun for maʿīn.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر العذاب، وهو مطلق، ذكر فقد ما به حياة النفوس وهو الماء، وهو عذاب مخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to “if He destroys me” is “who will protect you?” and the answer to “if your water sinks” is “who will bring you water?”
rows.anchor: وجواب إن أهلكني: فمن يجير، وجواب إن أصبح: فمن يأتيكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the verse was recited to a mocker who said souls and pickaxes could bring the water, the water of his eyes then went away.
rows.anchor: وتليت هذه الآية عند بعض المستهزئين فقال: تجيء به النفوس والمعاويل، فذهب ماء عينيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shawāʾ can mean human skin, an animal's limbs, any nonfatal body part, or by extension a loss of wealth or something slight; the cited verse uses shawāʾ for a body part.
rows.anchor: والشوى: جلد الإنسان، والشوى: قوائم الحيوان، والشوى: كل عضو ليس بمقتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ramā fa-ashwā means that the thrower missed the vital part.
rows.anchor: ومنه: رمى فأشوى، إذا لم يصب المقتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Halaʿ is rapid fear and agitation at hardship and rapid withholding when good arrives; the name is linked to a swift-moving she-camel.
rows.anchor: الهلع: الفزع والاضطراب السريع عند مسن المكروه، والمنع السريع عند مس الخير

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda defines halaʿ as the greatest greed and the worst anxiety.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الهلع في اللغة أشد الحرص وأسوأ الجزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jazaʿ means fear; a cited poetic line demonstrates the word.
rows.anchor: الجزع: الخوف، قال الشاعر: جزعت ولم أجزع من البين مجزعا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda explains ʿizīn as groups gathered in scattered fashion.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: جماعات في تفرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes ʿizīn to mean small groups, such as groups of three or four.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجمع اليسير كثلاثة ثلاثة وأربعة أربعة

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿi explains “in the house are ʿizūn” as meaning different groups of people; poetry by ʿAntara and others illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي: في الدار عزون: أي أصناف من الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿizza has an elided final radical, possibly wāw, from ʿazwa because each group affiliates with a different one; ʿazā yaʿzū means to attribute something to another.
rows.anchor: وعزة مما حذفت لامه، فقيل: هي واو وأصله عزوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the final radical is hāʾ and the original is ʿazaha; it takes a wāw-and-nūn plural like sana, with either kasra or ḍamma on the ʿayn.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لامها هاء والأصل عزهة وجمعت عزة بالواو والنون، كما جمعت سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line describes dawn breathing; the verb tanaffasa means air emerging from within, metaphorically dawn spreading until full daylight.
rows.anchor: التنفس: خروج النسيم من الجوف، واستعير للصبح ومعناه: امتداده حتى يصير نهارا واضحا

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba's verse uses taʿasʿasa to describe the night coming on.
rows.anchor: وقال رؤبة: يا هند ما أسرع ما تعسعسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍanīn means suspected and is faʿīl in the passive sense; it can also mean miserly, as a cited poem using ḍanīn demonstrates.
rows.anchor: الظنين: المتهم، فعيل بمعنى مفعول، ظننت الرجل: اتهمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line uses ḍanīn in the sense of stingy.
rows.anchor: والظنين: البخيل، قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is Meccan, and its connection to the preceding sūrah is very clear.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية. ومناسبتها لما قبلها في غاية الظهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas interprets the sun's being rolled up as its entering the Throne.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: إدخالها في العرش

rows.speaker: مجاهد، وقتادة، والحسن
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Hasan say the sun loses its light.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة والحسن: ذهاب ضوئها

rows.speaker: الربيع بن خيثم
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaytham says the sun is thrown away, connecting the word to “I rolled it and it rolled up.”
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن خيثم: رمى بها، ومنه: كورته فتكور

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih explains the sun as inverted.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: نكست

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A further report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the sun darkens.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: أظلمت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A further view from Mujahid says the sun fades away.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: اضمحلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views say the sun disappears, or that it is wrapped together and cast into the sea.
rows.anchor: وقيل: غورت وقيل: يلف بعضها ببعض ويرمي بها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda compares the sun's rolling to the wrapping of a turban.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: كورت مثل تكوير العمامة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubi derives the image from wrapping and gathering a turban, followed by the sun's light vanishing and its being thrown away.
rows.anchor: من كار العمامة على رأسه يكورها، أي لاثها وجمعها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses al-shams as the subject of an omitted verb explained by kuwwirat, since idhā calls for a verb due to its conditional meaning.
rows.anchor: بل على الفاعلية، رافعها فعل مضمر يفسره كورت، لأن إذا يطلب الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes that al-Zamakhshari calls the passive subject a subject by convention, but says his parsing is not compulsory: al-Akhfash and the Kufans allow a nominal clause after idhā.
rows.anchor: وليس ما ذكر من الإعراب مجمعا على تحتمه عند النحاة، بل يجوز رفع الشمس على الابتداء عند الأخفش والكوفيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿthara applied to goods means turning them upside down; baʿthara and baḥthara a basin mean demolishing it and reversing its top and bottom.
rows.anchor: بعثرت المتاع: قلبته ظهرا لبطن، وبعثرت الحوض وبحثرته: هدمته وجعلت أعلاه أسفله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is Meccan; the author says the meaning of infiṭār has already been discussed.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية. وانفطارها تقدم الكلام فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scattering of the stars means they fall from their places like beads falling from a necklace.
rows.anchor: وانتثار الكواكب: سقوطها من مواضعها كالنظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the doubled jīm in fujjirat; Mujahid and other named readers lighten it. On the intensive reading, the seas overflow because they are full, either spilling over or having their water removed by God.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فجرت بتشديد الجيم ومجاهد والربيع بن خيثم والزعفراني والثوري: بخفها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid's light reading can mean that the seas transgress because their barrier is removed, invoking the statement that the two seas do not transgress and the opposition between transgression and fujūr.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: فجرت مبنيا للفاعل مخففا بمعنى: بغت لزوال البرزخ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas explains buʿthirat as searched through.
rows.anchor: بعثرت، قال ابن عباس: بحثت

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the graves are stirred up to raise the dead.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: أثيرت لبعث الأموات

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says the earth's buried gold and silver are brought out.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: أخرج ما في بطنها من الذهب والفضة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats baʿthara and baḥthara as equivalent forms built from baʿth and baḥth with an added rāʾ, meaning that the dead are searched out and extracted.
rows.anchor: بعثر وبحثر بمعنى واحد، وهما مركبان من البعث والبحث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that derivation: rāʾ is not an augmentative letter, and the two words have different roots despite agreeing in meaning; he also mentions the sūrah al-Tawba's epithet al-Mubaʿthira for exposing hypocrites' secrets.
rows.anchor: والأمر ليس كما يقتضيه كلامه، لأن الراء ليست من حروف الزيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No soul's power to benefit another is general, as in the verse saying that on that day none of you can benefit or harm another.
rows.anchor: عام كقوله: فاليوم لا يملك بعضكم لبعض نفعا ولا ضرا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil narrows the meaning: no soul can provide any benefit to a disbelieving soul.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: لنفس كافرة شيئا من المنفعة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says sovereignty belongs to God today as well, but on Judgment Day no one will claim to rival Him, and He will not let anyone retain what he possessed in worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وكذلك هو اليوم، لكنه هناك لا يدعي أحد منازعة
